title: Sony Music moves to add more than 30,000 copyrighted recordings to its lawsuit against Udio

reading.body:
Udio, an AI music generation service, trained its models on recorded music without obtaining licenses from the rights holders. The core failure here is deployment of a generative system built on training data whose use was not authorized, a problem that existed at the point the models were assembled, before any user ever generated a song. Major labels alleged the system reproduced the character of specific copyrighted works, and the volume of recordings at issue, over 30,000 in Sony's claims alone, indicates the training pipeline drew broadly from commercially released catalogues.

The litigation produced divergent outcomes across different rights holders. Universal Music Group settled and entered a licensing arrangement requiring Udio to build a future platform trained only on authorized material, suggesting the original training corpus was not confined to licensed works. Warner Music Group followed a similar path. Sony Music pursued a separate new lawsuit after a court declined to let it expand its original case, and a class action brought by independent artists survived a dismissal motion and was transferred to a new jurisdiction. These are ongoing legal proceedings, not final findings, and no court has issued a verdict establishing that infringement occurred or assigning liability.

What the incident shows is that the question of what a model may lawfully be trained on was not resolved before the system launched to millions of users. A rights-clearance review conducted before training began would have been the point at which this class of problem could have been caught, because by the time a generative model is deployed the training decisions are already fixed.

summary:
Universal Music Group has settled a lawsuit against AI music startup Udio, reaching licensing agreements to resolve claims that Udio used copyrighted songs to train its artificial intelligence system. The case alleged that Udio improperly used tracks like The Temptations' "My Girl" to create similar music without permission or compensation. Under the settlement, Udio will launch a new platform next year trained exclusively on authorized and licensed music, allowing users to customize, stream, and share songs while compensating artists who participate.

This marks Udio's first major licensing agreement with a record label and represents a shift toward collaboration between AI companies and the music industry. Udio, founded in 2024 by former Google DeepMind employees, has attracted millions of users since its launch. The company declined to disclose financial terms of the settlement. Additionally, UMG announced a separate partnership with Stability AI to develop music creation tools for artists and producers, signaling broader efforts to integrate AI technology responsibly within the entertainment sector.
